analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and lets people buy into federal employee health plans at full price.
analysis.headline: The repeal-and-replace bill, introduced by Rep. Darrell Issa with zero cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in any of its nine committees and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the Affordable Care Act — its subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and market rules — starting two years after passage [S2][S3]. In its place, anyone not eligible for Medicaid, Medicare, or military coverage could buy the same health plans federal employees get, but with no government help paying the premium [S2][S3]. It would also create a new tax deduction for those premiums and repeal the health-related tax provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law, which include the 3.8% Medicare surtax on investment income [S3]. The bill was referred to nine House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress expired [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers would gain a new pool of full-premium customers through the federal employee plan system, and people with high investment income would gain from the repeal of the 3.8% Medicare surtax on unearned income [S3]. Some middle-income uninsured people could buy coverage with a new above-the-line tax deduction, but that deduction is worth more to people with higher tax bills [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Opens the Federal Employee Health Benefits Program to any individual who is not a federal employee, unless they are eligible for Medicaid, Medicare, CHIP, or another public program, are in the uniformed services, or are not lawfully present in the U.S. [S2][S3]
Bars FEHBP plans from imposing lifetime or annual dollar limits and from discriminating against licensed providers, and extends dependent coverage to age 26 within the program [S3]

Creates an above-the-line income tax deduction for premiums paid by non-employee FEHBP enrollees, and lets an employer contribute on the individual's behalf, though no government contribution is allowed [S2][S3]
Repeals the Affordable Care Act and the health-related provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law effective two years after enactment, restoring prior law as if they had never passed [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Low-income people who gain eligibility for Medicaid under the expansion would be barred from FEHBP enrollment and would lose that coverage route when the ACA is repealed [S2][S3]. Middle-class people currently receiving ACA premium subsidies would lose the subsidies and pay full price for coverage [S2]. People in the regular insurance market outside FEHBP would lose the ACA's protections — including guaranteed issue and the ban on pre-existing condition exclusions — because the bill restores the law as it stood before 2010 [S3]. People with investment income would keep paying the 3.8% surtax only because the bill failed [S3].

drawbacks.text: No government contribution is allowed for non-federal enrollees, so coverage would come at full premium cost; the bill instead offers a tax deduction, which does little for people who owe little or no income tax [S3]

Individuals enrolled in or eligible for Medicaid, Medicare, CHIP, or any other public program are barred from enrolling, so the very populations the ACA's expansion served would have no replacement coverage under the bill [S3]
Repealing the ACA and reviving prior law restores the pre-2010 individual insurance market outside FEHBP, where carriers could again deny coverage or charge more for pre-existing conditions [S3]

The bill's tax provisions repeal the health-related title of the 2010 reconciliation law, which includes the 3.8% Medicare tax on net investment income, delivering its largest tax benefit to high-income households [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — letting everyone buy the plans Congress members and federal workers get — is popular in principle, and the bill keeps a few real protections inside FEHBP, like no lifetime limits and coverage to age 26 [S3]. But the design undercuts the promise: premiums would be paid entirely out of pocket, enrollment is barred for anyone eligible for Medicaid or Medicare, and the ACA's repeal would return pre-existing-condition discrimination to the ordinary insurance market [S3]. Meanwhile the tax side, including repeal of the investment-income surtax, tilts toward higher earners [S3]. For most people who currently rely on ACA subsidies or Medicaid expansion, this bill would mean worse or no coverage, with the tax relief flowing in the other direction.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to nine House committees and two subcommittees, it never received a hearing or a vote, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) introduced the bill on March 7, 2017 [S1][S5]
No other member cosponsored it at any point [S4]

It was referred to nine committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Appropriations, House Administration, and Rules — and then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Natural Resources Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs Subcommittee [S5]
No further action was taken through the end of the Congress, so the bill died without ever being debated or voted on [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, nothing changed: people who rely on ACA subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and pre-existing-condition protections kept their coverage and protections, while health insurers and high-income households did not get the bill's new market and tax breaks. With zero cosponsors and no committee action, the bill's death reflected the absence of support rather than a fight.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held; the only signal of partisan shape is that a single Republican sponsored the bill and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would hand FEHBP carriers a new pool of non-federal enrollees paying full premiums, with a tax deduction to help cover the bill, while the ACA repeal would deregulate the rest of the market by restoring pre-2010 rules. Insurers would gain flexibility and full-price customers, though repeal of the individual mandate would shrink the pool of people buying coverage at all.

Repealing the health-related provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law would eliminate the 3.8% Medicare tax on net investment income, and the new premium deduction is worth the most to people with large tax bills. These gains come at the cost of the subsidies and market rules that protected people with less income.

industries.industry: People receiving ACA subsidies or Medicaid expansion coverage
industries.note: These households would lose premium subsidies and, if Medicaid-eligible, would be barred from the FEHBP replacement, leaving many with no affordable coverage option. They had nothing to gain and a lot to lose from passage.
